You are a skeptical source-verifier. Below is a JSON findings list from a research survey. For EACH finding: use WebSearch/WebFetch (load via ToolSearch with query "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" if needed) to confirm the named standard/framework/tool/paper actually exists and that "what_it_defines" and "form_elements" accurately describe it. Mark exists=false for anything you cannot confirm, accurately_described=false with corrections for anything misdescribed. Be strict: a plausible-sounding but unconfirmable citation must be marked exists=false.

FINDINGS JSON:
[{"name":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774:2021 — Specification for process description","tradition":"ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 + IEEE systems & software engineering","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774:2021, Systems and software engineering — Life cycle management — Specification for process description, 1st ed., May 2021 (supersedes ISO/IEC TR 24774:2010). Element structure verified against the standard's own preview text (clause 5 TOC).","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/78981.html","what_it_defines":"The meta-format for describing any process: which elements a process description contains, which are required vs optional, and rules for formulating each. Explicitly applicable to any process model or description developed for any purpose — it standardizes the description, not the process content, and prescribes no execution or workflow semantics.","form_elements":["REQUIRED: process name/title (verb-phrase label)","REQUIRED: process purpose (single high-level goal statement)","REQUIRED: process outcomes (short list of observable, assessable results — 'An X is produced/defined' declarative form)","OPTIONAL: process activities (cohesive groupings of tasks)","OPTIONAL: process tasks (individual requirements/recommendations/permissible actions)","OPTIONAL: notes","OPTIONAL: process inputs and process outputs","OPTIONAL: process controls and constraints","Process views/viewpoints (clause 6): alternative renderings of the same process set for a stakeholder concern","Conformance-claim rules (clause 7) for full vs tailored conformance to a described process"],"fit_notes":"Best single fit in the survey for the seed layer's process-definition format. It is definition-level by construction: purpose+outcomes carry 'expected outcomes/outputs' natively, and outcomes being observable/assessable is exactly the hook from which mechanical checks and review rubrics can be derived (the 330xx family does precisely this derivation). It deliberately says nothing about sequencing engines. Gap to cover by extension: no first-class 'resulting actions / termination condition' element for long-running loops — the controls-and-constraints and outcomes slots can host these, or borrow ETVX exit criteria. Cheap to emulate in Markdown/YAML; the standard itself is short.","adopt_potential":"adopt"},{"name":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 — life-cycle process outcome convention","tradition":"ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 + IEEE systems & software engineering","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, Systems and software engineering — System life cycle processes; ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017, Systems and software engineering — Software life cycle processes. Both write every process in the 24774 description convention and share a harmonized process model.","url":"https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/15288/10424/","what_it_defines":"Not a meta-format but the largest worked corpus OF the format: ~30 named life-cycle processes, each described as title, purpose, outcomes, then activities and tasks. Demonstrates the convention at scale, including how outcomes stay implementation-free while tasks carry shall/should-level prescription.","form_elements":["Per process: title","Per process: purpose statement (one sentence)","Per process: outcomes list (typically 3–8 declarative observable results)","Per process: activities, each decomposed into tasks (normative shall-statements)","Process categories/groups (agreement, organizational project-enabling, technical management, technical)","Notes linking processes to information items (documents) produced"],"fit_notes":"Useful as the style guide and worked-example library for writing shop process definitions in 24774 form — how to phrase outcomes so they are checkable, how to keep purpose distinct from outcomes, how activities/tasks nest without becoming a workflow. Do not adopt the content (system-engineering process catalog is the wrong domain and far too heavy); adopt the phrasing conventions. Describing, not recommending, the catalog itself.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"ISO/IEC 330xx process assessment family (ex-ISO/IEC 15504 / SPICE)","tradition":"ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 process assessment (SPICE lineage)","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO/IEC 33001:2015, Information technology — Process assessment — Concepts and terminology; ISO/IEC 33004:2015 — Requirements for process reference, process assessment and maturity models; (measurement framework in ISO/IEC 33020). Supersedes ISO/IEC 15504 as of March 2015.","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/54175.html","what_it_defines":"The formal architecture connecting process DEFINITIONS to process CHECKS: a Process Reference Model (PRM) describes each process only by purpose + outcomes (24774-conformant, explicitly free of capability/quality aspects); a Process Assessment Model (PAM) then maps assessment indicators — base practices and work products — onto those outcomes; a measurement framework adds process attributes rated on an N/P/L/F scale.","form_elements":["PRM: domain declaration + set of processes, each = purpose + outcomes only","Rule: PRM process descriptions must not embed capability-level or measurement aspects (separation of definition from assessment)","PAM: per-process assessment indicators — base practices (evidence an outcome is achieved) and work products (evidence artifacts)","Measurement framework: process attributes (e.g., PA1.1 process performance) with achievement rating scale","Capability/maturity levels built on attribute ratings"],"fit_notes":"The architectural pattern is the shop's re-founding principle stated as an international standard: construction definition (purpose+outcomes) comes first, and every check (indicator, rating) is derived from and traceable to it. Adapt the derivation pattern — outcomes → indicators → rubric — while rejecting the machinery (capability levels, assessor qualification, maturity staging) as enterprise-appraisal weight a lightweight LLM shop does not need. This is also the strongest external justification available for the shop's 'checks derived from definitions' stance.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"OMG SPEM 2.0 — Software & Systems Process Engineering Metamodel","tradition":"OMG modeling standards (UML/MOF family)","source_type":"standard","citation":"Object Management Group, Software & Systems Process Engineering Meta-Model Specification, Version 2.0, OMG document formal/08-04-01, April 2008.","url":"https://www.omg.org/spec/SPEM/2.0","what_it_defines":"A metamodel for defining methods, with a hard structural separation between Method Content (reusable definitions of who/what/how, with no ordering) and Process (selective reuse of that content arranged into lifecycles for a project type). The canonical statement that role/task/artifact definitions are assets independent of any sequencing.","form_elements":["Method Content: Role Definition (skills, responsibilities)","Method Content: Task Definition (with steps; performed-by role; input/output work products)","Method Content: Work Product Definition (artifact/deliverable/outcome kinds)","Method Content: Guidance — typed attachments including guideline, CHECKLIST, template, example, concept, report","Process side: Activity, Role Use, Task Use, Work Product Use — occurrences of content elements in an ordered structure","Process patterns for reusable process chunks","Managed textual descriptions attached to every element (purpose, brief description, main description)"],"fit_notes":"The method-content/process separation is a direct structural match for the shop: role prompts and discrete skills are Method Content; any process definition is a separate layer that references them — and SPEM proves you can maintain a full knowledge base of definitions 'without ever creating a process.' Checklist-as-first-class-guidance-type is also a precedent for attaching fitness-test sets to definitions. Adapt, don't adopt wholesale: the MOF/UML metamodel, compliance points, and XMI serialization are heavyweight tooling concerns; take the element taxonomy and the separation principle. Known weakness (which motivated Essence): SPEM has no semantic slot for outcomes/goals or progress/health — pair it with 24774-style outcomes.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Eclipse Process Framework (EPF) Composer / Unified Method Architecture","tradition":"Eclipse open-source tooling implementing SPEM (IBM RUP lineage)","source_type":"tool","citation":"Eclipse Process Framework Project (EPF), Eclipse Foundation; EPF Composer authoring tool implementing the UMA/SPEM 2.0 metamodel; ships the OpenUP method library as its exemplar.","url":"https://projects.eclipse.org/projects/technology.epf","what_it_defines":"The working proof of SPEM's separation: method plugins hold reusable role/task/work-product/guidance content; Capability Patterns are reusable process chunks; Delivery Processes are full lifecycles assembled by binding patterns. Publishes method content as a static HTML site — definitions as browsable documents, no engine.","form_elements":["Method library / method plugin packaging of content","Role, Task (with steps), Work Product, Guidance pages with standard description fields","Capability Pattern: reusable cluster of activities for one area of concern","Delivery Process: full lifecycle assembled from patterns via work-breakdown structure","Published static-site output of the whole method (content without execution)"],"fit_notes":"Context rather than adoption: the Eclipse tool itself is dormant Java tooling nobody should build on in 2026. Its value to the shop is as an existence proof and design reference — a mature system where definition documents (roles, tasks, artifacts, checklists) compile into an agent-consumable (here, human-consumable) corpus with processes strictly layered on top. The plugin/library packaging idea loosely parallels the shop's skills-plus-role-prompts compilation model.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Rational Unified Process (RUP) — role/activity/artifact static structure","tradition":"Rational/IBM software process engineering (predecessor of SPEM and EPF)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Kruchten, P., The Rational Unified Process: An Introduction, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 2003 — ch. 3 'Static Structure: Process Description' defines the element model; also IBM Rational Method Composer product documentation.","url":"https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/rational-unified-process/0321197704/ch03.html","what_it_defines":"The original commercial articulation of process-as-structured-content: 'who is doing what, how, and when' via Roles (who), Activities with steps (how), Artifacts (what), Workflows (when), grouped into Disciplines. Every artifact has a responsible role, a template, and review checkpoints; every role lists responsibilities and required skills.","form_elements":["Role: responsibilities + required competencies/skills","Activity: unit of work performed by one role, decomposed into steps (thinking/performing/reviewing)","Artifact: information element with exactly one responsible role, produced/consumed by activities; carries templates and checkpoints (review checklists)","Workflow: sequencing view over activities (kept separate from the definitions)","Discipline: skillset-based container grouping roles/activities/artifacts"],"fit_notes":"Historically the template everything else formalized (SPEM/EPF/UMA are its descendants), so mostly context. Two forms remain directly reusable: (a) the one-responsible-role-per-artifact rule, a clean accountability convention for artifact schema definitions; (b) artifact 'checkpoints' — per-artifact review checklists shipped with the artifact definition — a direct precedent for deriving review rubrics from artifact schemas. RUP's content is proprietary IBM material and its lifecycle prescriptions are irrelevant here.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"OMG Essence 1.2 — Kernel and Language for Software Engineering Methods (SEMAT)","tradition":"OMG / SEMAT initiative (Jacobson et al.)","source_type":"standard","citation":"Object Management Group, Essence — Kernel and Language for Software Engineering Methods, Version 1.2, OMG document formal/18-10-02, 2018; Essence 2.0 in beta at OMG as of 2025.","url":"https://www.omg.org/spec/Essence/1.2/About-Essence","what_it_defines":"A standard for defining practices and methods around progress and health rather than workflow: Alphas (essential things whose state you track) each have an ordered set of named states, and each state carries a short qualitative CHECKLIST; Activity Spaces name essential things to do; Competencies name required capabilities with levels; a composition language assembles practices into methods.","form_elements":["Alpha: essential trackable concern (kernel's seven: Opportunity, Stakeholders, Requirements, Software System, Team, Work, Way of Working)","Alpha state: named progress/health state with a checklist of a few plainly-worded criteria per state","Work product: described artifact with levels of detail, attached to alphas as evidence","Activity: has completion criteria expressed in terms of alpha states and work-product levels of detail — i.e., termination conditions defined by state, not by step count","Activity space: placeholder for essential work, method-agnostic","Competency: capability with five achievement levels","Practice/Method: composable units — a method is a composition of practices over the kernel","Card-based presentation format (state cards with checklists) designed for at-a-glance use"],"fit_notes":"The strongest external answer to two of the seed layer's hardest requirements. (a) Small qualitative fitness-test sets for non-deterministic output: alpha-state checklists are exactly that form, standardized — short, ordinal, qualitative, judged not computed. (b) Termination for long-running loops: Essence activities complete when target alpha states are reached, which is a definition-level termination semantic needing no engine. Adapt rather than adopt: keep the state+checklist+completion-criteria FORM, replace the software-endeavor kernel alphas with shop-native ones (e.g., Intent, Scenario Set, Dispatch, Reconciliation). Recent literature already explores LLM agents consuming Essence practice descriptions.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"CMMI model structure — goals/practices (V1.3) and practice areas with intent/value (V3.0)","tradition":"SEI/Carnegie Mellon capability maturity tradition, now ISACA","source_type":"framework","citation":"CMMI for Development, Version 1.3, CMU/SEI-2010-TR-033, Software Engineering Institute, 2010 (process area = purpose statement, specific goals/practices, generic goals/practices, informative subpractices and example work products); CMMI Model V3.0, ISACA, 2023 (practice areas with intent/value statements and practice-group levels).","url":"https://cybersigmacs.com/knowledge-center/cmmi/","what_it_defines":"A model format built on a required/expected/informative trichotomy: goals (required — what must be true) are distinct from practices (expected — typical ways to achieve them), which are distinct from informative material (subpractices, example work products). V3.0 recast this as practice areas carrying an intent statement + value statement + required info, with practices in evolutionary practice-group levels.","form_elements":["Process area / practice area: named cluster with purpose or intent statement","V3.0: value statement per practice area and per practice (why it matters, outcome-linked)","Specific goals (required component) vs specific practices (expected component) — achievement of the goal, not performance of the practice, is what is assessed","Generic goals/practices: institutionalization criteria applied uniformly across areas","Informative components: subpractices, notes, example work products, elaborations","V3.0 practice group levels 1–5: evolutionary layering where each level subsumes the lower"],"fit_notes":"Two adaptable forms: (a) the required/expected/informative trichotomy is a precise instrument for the shop's definitions — separating what must be true of a construction (checkable) from typical ways to construct it (guidance) prevents rubrics from ossifying implementation detail; (b) V3.0's intent+value statement pair is a compact established header for any definition. Reject the surrounding machinery (maturity levels, appraisal method, organizational institutionalization) as scale-inappropriate; CMMI is an appraisal model, not a process-definition format, so it earns adapt only for these structural devices.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"ITIL process description format (v3) and ITIL 4 practice guides","tradition":"UK OGC / AXELOS / PeopleCert IT service management","source_type":"framework","citation":"ITIL Service Design, 2011 edition, Cabinet Office/TSO (per-process description convention: purpose/objectives, scope, value, policies, activities, triggers/inputs/outputs/interfaces, CSFs/KPIs, roles); ITIL Foundation: ITIL 4 Edition, AXELOS, 2019, and the PeopleCert ITIL 4 practice guides (34 management practices).","url":"https://www.peoplecert.org/news-and-announcements/2023/itil-practice-guides-a-hidden-gem","what_it_defines":"v3: a fixed per-process documentation template — every process described with the same section skeleton including measurable success criteria. ITIL 4: replaced 'processes' with 'practices' (capability bundles), each documented in a standard practice-guide structure spanning the four dimensions of service management.","form_elements":["v3 per process: purpose and objectives; scope; value to business; policies/principles/basic concepts; process activities, methods, techniques; triggers, inputs, outputs, interfaces to other processes; information management; critical success factors (CSFs) with key performance indicators (KPIs) nested under each; challenges and risks","Roles bound via responsibility (RACI) matrices rather than embedded in the process text","ITIL 4 per practice guide: general information (purpose, key terms, practice success factors with key metrics); value streams and processes (activities with inputs/outputs, value-stream contribution); organizations and people (roles, competency profiles); information and technology; partners and suppliers"],"fit_notes":"Describing more than recommending: ITIL's template discipline — every process/practice documented in the identical section skeleton, with success factors and metrics nested under the definition — is a good pattern precedent, and its trigger element covers the seed layer's 'resulting actions' need better than the ISO line does. Its practice-success-factor → key-metric nesting is another instance of checks-derived-from-definitions. Reasons to only adapt: content is IT-operations-specific, the corpus is commercial/licensed (not freely citable text), and ITIL 4's practice guides are long-form prose, heavier than a lightweight seed layer wants.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289 — Content of life-cycle information items (documentation)","tradition":"ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 + IEEE systems & software engineering","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO/IEC/IEEE 15289:2019, Systems and software engineering — Content of life-cycle information items (documentation), 4th ed. (earlier editions 2011, 2015, 2017).","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/74909.html","what_it_defines":"The standard meta-format for artifact/document-type schemas: every information item is classified as one of seven generic document types, and then given specific required-content clauses. Explicitly medium-independent — an information item may live in a repository, be split, or be combined; the schema defines content, not packaging.","form_elements":["Seven generic types: description, plan, policy, procedure, report, request, specification","Generic content requirements per type (e.g., every plan carries scope, approach, schedule, resources, risks)","Specific content requirements per named information item (e.g., what a test plan or an architecture description must contain)","Mapping tables from information items to the 12207/15288 processes that produce/consume them","Rule that items are defined 'as if a separate document' but may be aggregated or stored as records"],"fit_notes":"Direct adopt for the artifact/document-type schema slot in the seed layer: the two-level scheme (generic type → specific required content) is exactly a document schema definition, and the process↔information-item mapping tables are the established way to state 'this process yields these artifacts' — tying process outcomes to artifact schemas so checks can validate both together. The shop's existing kind-schema/template mechanism (write-* skills) is already isomorphic to this; 15289 supplies the external standard to anchor it. Its specific item catalog (test plans, QA records) is domain content to ignore.","adopt_potential":"adopt"},{"name":"ETVX — Entry / Task / Verification / eXit process-definition paradigm","tradition":"IBM programming process architecture (CMM-era process definition)","source_type":"paper","citation":"Radice, R.A., Roth, N.K., O'Hara, A.C., Ciarfella, W.A., 'A Programming Process Architecture', IBM Systems Journal, vol. 24, no. 2, 1985 — origin of the ETVX paradigm, widely reused in SEI/CMM-lineage process definition guidance.","url":"https://sceweb.sce.uhcl.edu/helm/REQ_ENG_WEB/My-Files/mod1/swdev_proc_kernel/SoftwareProcessKernels.pdf","what_it_defines":"The minimal per-activity definition cell: Entry criteria that must hold before work starts; the Task set; Verification steps confirming the right tasks were done right; eXit criteria that must hold for the activity to be complete. Composable into larger processes by chaining cells; no ordering engine implied.","form_elements":["Entry criteria (preconditions on inputs/state, including triggers)","Task list (what is performed)","Verification/validation conditions (checks bound to the tasks)","Exit criteria (postconditions/outputs that define 'done')"],"fit_notes":"The lightest credible established form in the survey, and the only classic one that builds verification INTO the definition cell — matching 'definitions precede checks' at the single-activity grain. Exit criteria are a ready-made termination construct for long-running loops (loop until exit criteria hold), and entry criteria give 'resulting actions' their trigger side. Adopt as the per-activity inner structure inside 24774-style process definitions (24774 gives the process header — purpose/outcomes; ETVX gives each activity its entry/verify/exit contract). Caveat: primary 1985 paper is paywalled IBM Systems Journal material; the paradigm itself is thoroughly documented in secondary process-engineering literature.","adopt_potential":"adopt"},{"name":"BPMN 2.0 — Business Process Model and Notation (definition-level positioning)","tradition":"OMG business modeling / ISO adoption","source_type":"standard","citation":"OMG, Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0, formal/2011-01-03; published as ISO/IEC 19510:2013. Conformance clause distinguishes Process Modeling Conformance (descriptive/analytic sub-classes) from Process Execution Conformance.","url":"https://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/2.0/","what_it_defines":"A graphical notation plus XML interchange format for control-flow process models: activities, events, gateways, sequence/message flows, pools/lanes, data objects. The spec itself stratifies usage — a Descriptive conformance sub-class exists precisely for documentation-level modeling with no execution semantics exercised.","form_elements":["Flow objects: activities/tasks, events (start/intermediate/end, incl. timer/message/error), gateways (exclusive/parallel/inclusive/event-based)","Swimlanes: pools and lanes assigning flow to participants/roles","Data objects, data stores, messages","Sequence flow and message flow connectors","Descriptive vs Analytic vs Common Executable conformance sub-classes","XML process-definition interchange format"],"fit_notes":"Context-only, on the task's own framing. BPMN answers 'in what order does control flow' — it has no slots for purpose, outcomes, quality criteria, or role/artifact definitions, so it cannot carry a construction definition; and its center of gravity (execution semantics, engine interchange) is exactly the workflow-engine prescription the shop is avoiding. Legitimate residual use: an occasional descriptive-class diagram inside a process definition when a handoff topology genuinely needs a picture — mermaid can render the equivalent without importing the standard.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"CMMN — Case Management Model and Notation","tradition":"OMG business modeling (declarative counterpart to BPMN)","source_type":"standard","citation":"OMG, Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN), Version 1.0, 2014 (current version 1.1 at omg.org/spec/CMMN); introductory treatment in Marin, 'Introduction to the Case Management Model and Notation (CMMN)', arXiv:1608.05011, 2016.","url":"https://www.omg.org/spec/CMMN/","what_it_defines":"A declarative model for knowledge work where activity order is unpredictable: a case plan contains stages and tasks whose availability is governed by sentries (entry criteria) and exit criteria, plus milestones marking achieved states and discretionary items a knowledge worker may add at run time. Describes what is allowed/required, never a flow sequence.","form_elements":["Case plan model containing stages (nestable) and tasks (human, process, case, decision)","Sentries: entry criteria and exit criteria on any plan item, combining events and conditions","Milestones: named achievable states with entry criteria (no work of their own)","Event listeners (timer, user)","Discretionary items and planning tables (run-time plan extension)","Case file items: the information the case works over"],"fit_notes":"Context-only as a notation to adopt (thin industry uptake, engine-flavored spec), but it is the standards world's clearest vocabulary for exactly the shop's situation: long-running, non-deterministic work defined by entry/exit criteria and milestones rather than sequences. Worth mining terminologically — 'milestone with entry criteria' and 'exit criterion on a stage' are precise, citable concepts for expressing loop termination and resulting actions in process definitions without any flow prescription. If a definition-level format for unpredictable work is ever needed wholesale, CMMN is the precedent to cite.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"IDEF0 — Integration Definition for Function Modeling (ICOM)","tradition":"US Air Force SADT lineage / NIST federal standard","source_type":"standard","citation":"NIST, Integration Definition for Function Modeling (IDEF0), FIPS PUB 183, 1993; also IEEE Std 1320.1-1998 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 31320-1:2012.","url":"https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/FIPS/fipspub183.pdf","what_it_defines":"A function-decomposition format: each function is a box with typed arrows — Inputs (left, transformed), Controls (top, constrain/govern), Outputs (right, results), Mechanisms (bottom, who/what performs) — decomposed hierarchically (A0, A1, A11…) with strict syntax rules. Models what functions exist and what they consume/produce/obey, not when they run.","form_elements":["Function box with verb-phrase name","ICOM arrows: Input, Control, Output, Mechanism (and Call)","Hierarchical decomposition with parent-child diagram numbering and arrow continuity rules","Node tree and glossary as required companion artifacts","Rule set limiting boxes per diagram (3–6) to force appropriate altitude"],"fit_notes":"Context-only. Genuinely definition-level and engine-free, and the Control-vs-Input distinction (a definition or policy that GOVERNS an activity vs material it transforms) is a conceptually sharp device — the shop's construction definitions are, in IDEF0 terms, Controls compiled into the generating agent's context. But it is a diagram grammar without purpose/outcome/quality elements, its practitioner base has aged out, and adopting it would add notation burden with no checking leverage. Useful as vocabulary, not as a format.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"PMBOK Guide ITTO process format (PMI)","tradition":"Project Management Institute","source_type":"framework","citation":"Project Management Institute, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide), Sixth Edition, 2017 — 49 processes each defined by Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs; superseded in emphasis by PMBOK Seventh Edition, 2021 (principles and performance domains, ITTOs dropped from the core).","url":"https://www.brainbok.com/itto-pmp-and-itto-capm","what_it_defines":"Each process = a purpose paragraph plus three lists: Inputs (documents/plans consumed), Tools & Techniques (methods applied), Outputs (deliverables produced), with outputs of one process feeding inputs of others across five process groups and ten knowledge areas.","form_elements":["Process purpose paragraph","Inputs list","Tools & techniques list","Outputs list","Cross-process input/output tracing (data-flow diagrams per process)"],"fit_notes":"Context-only. The ITTO frame is widely known and trivially lightweight, but it defines a process by its I/O signature alone — no outcomes, no completion or quality criteria, nothing derivable into checks — and PMI itself walked away from it in the Seventh Edition, which is a caution against adopting it now. Its one durable idea, explicit output-to-input tracing between processes, is already covered better by 15289's process↔information-item mapping.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"ISO/IEC 24744 — Metamodel for Development Methodologies (SEMDM)","tradition":"ISO/IEC JTC1/SC7 method engineering (academic method-engineering community)","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO/IEC 24744:2014, Software engineering — Metamodel for development methodologies (first edition 2007), defining SEMDM via the powertype pattern.","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/62644.html","what_it_defines":"A rival metamodel to SPEM that models the method domain AND the endeavor domain together: powertype pairs (e.g., WorkProductKind/WorkProduct) let one define both the kind (the schema, at method level) and the instances produced when the method is enacted, covering work units, work products, producers (roles/tools), and stages in one framework.","form_elements":["Powertype pattern: paired Kind class (method level) and instance class (endeavor level) for every concept","Work units (tasks, techniques, processes)","Work products with kinds and status","Producers: roles, teams, tools","Stages: temporal method elements (phases, milestones) kept distinct from work units"],"fit_notes":"Context-only. Intellectually it addresses a problem the shop actually has — the same definition must both instruct generation (method level) and validate the generated instance (endeavor level), which is the powertype's exact job — so it is worth knowing the argument. But adoption fails the lightweight test decisively: SEMDM's uptake is essentially academic, tooling is nil, and its rigor overhead dwarfs the seed layer's needs. Cite it, if at all, as justification that definition-level and instance-level views of one concept belong in one artifact.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Scrum Guide accountabilities and artifact commitments (Definition of Done)","tradition":"Agile / Scrum (Schwaber & Sutherland)","source_type":"practice","citation":"Schwaber, K. and Sutherland, J., The Scrum Guide, November 2020, scrumguides.org — accountabilities replacing 'roles'; each artifact bound to a commitment (Product Goal, Sprint Goal, Definition of Done), with the Definition of Done as 'a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required'.","url":"https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html","what_it_defines":"Two compact definitional forms inside a deliberately minimal framework document: (a) role definitions as short accountability lists — each accountability a bullet of what the holder is answerable for, not a task script; (b) every artifact paired with exactly one commitment — a small, binding qualitative criteria set that says when the artifact is acceptable, with DoD as the canonical example.","form_elements":["Accountability list per role (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers): 4–8 bullets of answerable-for statements","Artifact + commitment pairing: Product Backlog→Product Goal, Sprint Backlog→Sprint Goal, Increment→Definition of Done","Definition of Done: enumerated qualitative quality measures; work not meeting it cannot be released and returns to the backlog (a built-in resulting-action rule)","Framework-level rule that the whole definition fits in ~13 pages (a lightness benchmark)"],"fit_notes":"Adapt. The artifact-plus-commitment pairing is the most widely operated real-world instance of the shop's exact pattern: a small qualitative fitness-test set attached to an artifact type, consulted by the producer during construction and by reviewers after — with a defined consequence when it fails (return to backlog = the resulting-action clause the seed layer wants). The accountability-list form is likewise a proven lightweight shape for role definitions feeding role prompts. These are practice forms, not schemas — pair them with 15289-style content schemas rather than replacing them.","adopt_potential":"adapt"}]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. ## ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 - System Life Cycle Processes

ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 establishes a common framework of process descriptions for describing the life cycle of systems. It concerns systems that can be configured with one or more of the following system elements: hardware elements, software elements, data, humans, processes, services, procedures, facilities, materials, and naturally occurring entities.

## ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 - Software Life Cycle Processes

ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 is an international standard for software lifecycle processes that aims to be a primary standard defining all the processes required for developing and maintaining software systems, including the outcomes and/or activities of each process. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207:2017 also provides processes that can be employed for defining, controlling, and improving software life cycle processes within an organization or a project.

## Relationship and Key Differences

Processes in both documents have the same process purpose and process outcomes, but differ in activities and tasks to perform software engineering or systems engineering, respectively. The processes, activities, and tasks of this document can also be applied during the acquisition of a system that contains software, either alone or in conjunction with ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2015, Systems and software engineering—System life cycle processes.

# Eclipse Process Framework Project

## Project Status
**The project is archived.** A warning message at the top of the page states: "This project is archived. Some links on this page may not work." The latest release was version 1.5.2 from April 2018.

## Overview
EPF is a framework for software process engineering that enables organizations to create, manage, and publish development methodologies. It consists of two main components:

**Framework Components:**
- A meta-model for structuring method content and processes
- Core extensible tooling for method authoring, process design, library management, and content publishing

## Key Relationships
The framework is built on standards including the OMG's "Software Process Engineering Meta-model (SPEM)" and IBM's Unified Method Architecture (UMA). As the documentation notes, "The initial version of this meta-model has been derived from IBM's Unified Method Architecture (UMA)."

## Core Capabilities
EPF Composer (the exemplary tool implementation) supports:
- Defining reusable method elements (roles, tasks, work products, guidance)
- Creating **capability patterns**—reusable process chunks applicable across multiple workflows
- Structuring **delivery processes** as end-to-end methodology flows
- Publishing configured processes as navigable HTML websites viewable without server infrastructure

The project included OpenUP as exemplary content, though development has ceased.

## PMBOK 6th Edition (2017)
The PMBOK® Guide – 6th edition outlines 5 process groups, 10 knowledge areas, and 49 processes. In the PMBOK 6th edition, these models, methods and artifacts were shown as inputs, tools and techniques and outputs (also known as ITTOs) of each process within a knowledge area.

## PMBOK 7th Edition (2021) Key Changes
The Standard for Project Management enumerates 12 principles of project management and the PMBOK® Guide – Seventh Edition is structured around eight project performance domains. 

The structural shift was significant: In the 7th edition, there are separate sections on models, methods and artifacts. Therefore, there is now a shift towards organizing methods and artifacts based on their purpose or intended outcome rather than just listing them as part of the ITTOs.

In summary, the 7th Edition moved away from the detailed process-based approach of the 6th Edition (with its 49 processes organized by knowledge areas and ITTOs) to a principles-based and performance domain-focused structure with 12 guiding principles and 8 performance domains.

## ITIL 4's 34 Management Practices

ITIL 4 defines 34 management practices that replace the process-focused approach used in earlier versions of ITIL. The 34 ITIL 4 management practices are divided into three categories: 14 General Management Practices, 17 Service Management Practices, and 3 Technical Management Practices.

## Four Dimensions of Service Management

The four dimensions of service management in ITIL 4 are: Organizations and People, Information and Technology, Partners and Suppliers, and Value Streams and Processes. Together, they help ensure a balanced and holistic approach to service management.

## Practice Guide Structure

All practice guides follow a consistent, standardised format, simplifying the search for similar content across all 34 practices. The practice guide sections include: About this document, General information, Value streams and processes, Organisations and people, Information and technology, and Partners and suppliers.

## Practice Success Factors

ITIL 4 includes 34 management practices as "sets of organizational resources designed for performing work or accomplishing an objective". For each practice, ITIL 4 provides various types of guidance, such as key terms and concepts, success factors.

Each practice guide includes detailed information on what a practice does and how it does it.

checks.corrections: Verified against the standard's own preview PDF (iTeh sample of ISO/IEC/IEEE 24774:2021). Almost everything checks out: first edition May 2021; cancels and replaces ISO/IEC TR 24774:2010; clause 5.3 required elements are process name (5.3.2), purpose (5.3.3), outcomes (5.3.4) — 'the minimum required elements for a process description shall be the name, purpose, and outcomes'; clause 5.4 optional elements are activities, tasks, notes, inputs, outputs, and controls and constraints (5.4.2–5.4.7); clause 6 is 'Process views and viewpoints'; clause 7 is 'Claims of conformance to a process'. ONE ERROR: the finding calls the process name a 'verb-phrase label'. The standard prescribes the opposite — a descriptive NOUN phrase (secondary sources quoting the standard: 'A descriptive noun phrase – the name of the process – is more useful... Wordy noun-verb or verb-noun phrases can get confused with process activities'), with names conventionally ending in the word 'process'. Verb phrases belong to activities/tasks, not the process name. Also unverifiable from the preview: the 'full vs tailored conformance' characterization of clause 7 (clause title confirmed, full/tailored wording not confirmed — that distinction is native to 15288/12207 conformance clauses).
